When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense.
  • According to recent reports, in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R.
  • The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. New research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

According to recent reports, in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together.

Different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh says.

The researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree.

To explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

During the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

The results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions swiftly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

In a recent development, if dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

The idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

"While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole.".

Breaking: How cognitive behavioral therapy works to treat OCD

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • It has been revealed that obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next.
  • Recent findings suggest that what unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It has been revealed that obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next. For some people, it’s checking the locks again and again, even when they know the door is shut. For others, it’s washing their hands until they feel clean, counting steps or objects, arranging things until they feel just right, or getting stuck on an unwanted thought.

Recent findings suggest that what unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop. But the relief doesn’t last and you end up back at the anxious thought, triggering the process again. For people living with OCD, this cycle can be exhausting.

Recent findings suggest that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most studied ways to break the OCD cycle, and one type in particular, called exposure and response prevention (ERP), has the strongest research support of any talk therapy for OCD. Here’s a look at what CBT for OCD involves, how ERP works, and what a session can feel like.

CBT is a structured, evidence-based form of talk therapy. It looks at how your thoughts, feelings, and actions feed each other, and it focuses on the present rather than digging through your past. Most versions help you notice unhelpful thoughts and respond to them in fresh ways.

It has been revealed that CBT for OCD works a little differently. With something like anxiety or low mood, a therapist might help you question a worried thought and look for more balanced evidence. With OCD, that technique can backfire. Trying to argue with an intrusive thought, or prove it wrong, can become a mental compulsion, which keeps the cycle going.

So OCD-focused CBT spends less time debating the content of your thoughts and more time changing how you respond to them. The main tool for that is ERP, a type of CBT that focuses on behavior.

If you've ever been told to "just stop worrying," you may know that advice doesn’t work for OCD. The cycle doesn’t respond to willpower alone.

Here's how the loop tends to run:.

You get an intrusive thought or fear you don’t want (the obsession).

To get relief, you do something to make the feeling go away (the compulsion), like checking, washing, asking for reassurance, or going over events in your mind.

You feel better, but only for a short while.

Each compulsion can teach your brain that the thought was a true threat and that the ritual kept you safe. So the thought tends to return.

According to recent reports, say you’re leaving for work. A thought pops up: What if I left the stove on? Your anxiety spikes, so you go back and check. The stove is off, and you feel relief. But on your way to the car, the doubt returns, along with the urge to check again.

That's why OCD can feel impossible to overcome. The very thing that calms you in the moment is what feeds the cycle.

ERP involves gradually facing the things that trigger your fears, while holding off on the compulsion. It can sound intimidating, but it’s planned and step by step, and you and your therapist agree on each move together. Here’s what it tends to look like.

A lot of questions up front: Early sessions are mostly about getting clear on what's happening. Expect to talk through your intrusive thoughts, the compulsions they trigger, and the situations you avoid.

Building a fear ladder: Your triggers get ranked from mild to most distressing, and you start near the bottom. You won't be asked to face your worst fear on day one.

Facing triggers on purpose: You'll meet a fear instead of dodging it, whether that's touching a doorknob, writing down a feared word, or sitting with an uncertain thought.

Not doing the compulsion: Expect to resist the response you'd normally reach for, even something subtle like seeking reassurance.

Industry observers note that sitting with the discomfort: At first the fear climbs, which can feel like proof it won't stop. Over time, many people find the fear eases, and they learn they can cope with it.

Homework between sessions: Practice between sessions is a big part of progress, so expect to take exposures home and work on them in your daily life.

ERP with a trained therapist is the core of OCD treatment, and nothing below replaces it. But the stretches between sessions can be long, and a few grounding habits may make them easier to deal with.

Mindfulness and meditation can help you practice noticing a thought, letting it pass, and not acting on it or trying to prove it wrong. That fits well with ERP, where you also learn to let urges be present without giving in. A few minutes a day can be a gentle place to start.

Sources indicate that one caution: if you catch yourself meditating to “cancel out” a bad thought, that’s the compulsion sneaking back in. The aim is to let thoughts come and go, not to get rid of them.

💙 Practice noticing a thought and letting it pass with Chibs Okereke’s short Working With Thoughts meditation.

When you’re struggling with anxiety or a racing heart, slow breathing can help your body settle. Box breathing is one option, since the even count gives your mind something simple to hold onto.

Sources indicate that use it for everyday stress, like after a tough commute or before bed. During an exposure, or when you’re trying to make a thought go away, it can work against ERP, because the point is to practice facing the discomfort. Ask your therapist when it’s okay to use it alongside your ERP practice.

💙 For a tense, jittery day, Panic SOS with Kirat Randhawa uses sight, sound, and touch to help your body settle.

Sources indicate that poor sleep and OCD symptoms often go hand in hand. Research links poor sleep to more intrusive thoughts and harder-to-manage symptoms. Rest may also make it easier to do your ERP practice.

A steady routine can help. Go to bed and wake up at about the same time each day, and dim the lights and put screens away 30 minutes or so before bed. A warm shower, gentle stretching, or a sleep meditation can help you unwind, and limiting caffeine later in the day may make it easier to fall asleep.

Sources indicate that bedtime can be a hard time for those of us with OCD, as quiet moments can leave room for intrusive thoughts, checking, or reassurance-seeking. If rituals are keeping you up, mention it to your therapist.

💙 Give your mind permission to power down with this Wind Down (for Sleep) session on Calm.

In a recent development, putting your obsessions, compulsions, and triggers on paper may help you and your therapist spot patterns you’d otherwise miss. Many people find it easiest to jot down a few quick notes each time the loop highlights up: what set it off, what thought or fear came up, what you did in response, and how you felt afterward. Over time, you may notice that certain places, times of day, or moods make the cycle more likely.

While you’re mapping the loop, try not to judge yourself or over-analyze your entries.

💙 If you’re struggling to get started, journaling prompts can help.

Industry observers note that A walk around the block, a stretch, or a few minutes of dancing in your kitchen can help ease stress and give your body a reset. Pick something that feels possible even on a hard day, and tie it to something you already do, like a few minutes of movement while your coffee brews or after you hang up a call. Doing it at about the same time each day can also help it stick.

One thing to watch for: if movement starts to feel like a ritual, like needing to take a certain number of steps or repeat a routine until it feels “just right,” mention it to your therapist.

💙 Tamara Levitt’s Mindful Walking series turns a short stroll into a chance to notice what’s around you.

OCD can be isolating. Talking with a friend or family member you trust can remind you that you’re more than your symptoms. If a loved one wants to help, ask your therapist how. Well-meaning support, like answering the same reassurance question again and again, can accidentally keep the cycle going, and a therapist can guide you both.

Recent findings suggest that A peer support group can also help. Reputable OCD organizations run groups where you can meet people doing the same work.

In a recent development, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most effective treatments for OCD, especially a type called exposure and response prevention (ERP). Research shows it can reduce symptoms for many people.

According to recent reports, CBT helps by targeting the anxiety cycle that keeps OCD going. Depending on how severe symptoms are, it's used on its own or alongside medication.

Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the best-studied therapy for OCD, but it isn’t the only option. Other approaches include cognitive therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and inference-based CBT (I-CBT). Cognitive therapy helps you examine the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel threatening. ACT focuses on making room for uncomfortable thoughts rather than fighting them. I-CBT targets the reasoning that makes an obsession feel believable. Medication, usually a type of antidepressant called an SSRI, is a separate treatment that can lower the intensity of symptoms. It’s often combined with therapy. A clinician can help you weigh which mix fits your situation.

Sources indicate that ERP, or exposure and response prevention, is a type of CBT where you gradually face your triggers while resisting the urge to do a compulsion. It's a first-line treatment for OCD.

It has been revealed that each time you sit with a fear and resist the ritual, your brain gets evidence that the feared outcome doesn't arrive and that the distress is survivable. That learning is what loosens OCD's grip. A therapist structures the exposures so they stay challenging without tipping into overwhelming.

The main difference is what each approach targets. Regular CBT often focuses on changing unhelpful thoughts, such as questioning a worry and replacing it with a more balanced one. CBT for OCD focuses on the compulsion.

Recent findings suggest that that’s because, with OCD, the compulsion is what keeps the cycle going. Each time you do the ritual, or try to prove the fear wrong, your brain learns that the thought was a real threat and the ritual kept you safe. In ERP, you face the trigger and hold off on the compulsion. Over time, your brain learns that the feared outcome doesn’t happen and that you can cope with the anxiety without the ritual. Some therapists also work on the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel so threatening, but ERP is the main tool.

Recent findings suggest that cognitive distortions are unhelpful thinking patterns, and in OCD they often show up as beliefs that make ordinary doubts feel dangerous. Common examples include:.

Feeling responsible for preventing harm, even when it’s unlikely.

Overestimating how likely something bad is to happen.

Thought-action fusion, or believing a thought is as bad as an action.

Struggling with not knowing for sure (intolerance of uncertainty).

Assuming a thought must matter because you had it.

Industry observers note that these patterns are common in OCD, and they can fuel the urge to do compulsions. Therapy can help you spot them and loosen their grip.

💙 Find out more about cognitive distortions and how to reframe negative thoughts.

It has been revealed that many people see meaningful improvement from ERP within about 12–20 sessions, which is often three to four months with weekly visits (intensive programs can be faster). Some notice shifts with fewer sessions, especially with regular practice in between.

Industry observers note that timelines vary with symptom severity, how often you practice, and whether medication is part of the initiative. OCD treatment is usually designed to be relatively short-term and skills-based, not open-ended.

You can do some ERP on your own, and self-help books and apps exist for it, but working with a trained therapist is strongly recommended, especially for moderate to severe OCD.

Self-directed ERP can be tricky to get right. It can be easy to accidentally turn an exposure into a subtle compulsion, or to skip the exposures that matter most. A therapist keeps the plan honest and adjusts it as you go. If therapy isn't available right now, guided self-help from a reputable OCD organization is a safer starting point than going it fully alone.

Mindfulness can support OCD treatment, but it isn't a standalone fix. Research on mindfulness for OCD is promising but mixed, and ERP remains the first-line treatment.

It has been revealed that on its own, mindfulness won't switch off intrusive thoughts, and expecting it to can backfire. Its real value is helping you relate to those thoughts differently, which is why it pairs with therapy rather than replacing it. A clinician can point you toward using it in a way that helps.

💙 If you’d like to try it, these tips for practicing mindfulness meditation are a gentle place to start.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.
  • One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.
  • Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, said:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that coffee may affect far more than alertness.
  • Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.
  • The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that coffee may affect far more than alertness. Fresh research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.

Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.

How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection.

Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.

Industry observers note that the fresh research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.

Researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.

For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.

What Happened When Coffee Was Removed.

According to recent reports, the regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.

When coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.

Coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.

After coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.

Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria.

Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.

According to recent reports, bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.

Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.

Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.

Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Highlighted Different Effects.

One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.

Improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.

It has been revealed that coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.

Industry observers note that caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.

It has been revealed that because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide latest clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.

Recent findings suggest that corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.

"Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet.".

The findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.

"Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," stated Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

Sources indicate that the mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

In a recent development, the type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

Spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

The identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron states the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

Sources indicate that saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert upcoming audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz notes the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone.
  • Industry observers note that latest research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone. The faces that capture a child's attention could provide vital clues about their mental health and how depression develops.

Industry observers note that latest research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces. The pattern appears to differ depending on whether a child has a family history of depression.

Industry observers note that researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time. By identifying these patterns while children are still developing, scientists hope to better understand who may be at greater risk and eventually improve prevention strategies.

Sources indicate that "Most of the vulnerabilities that we focus on are still developing during this time period," said Brandon Gibb, director of the Mood Disorders Institute and SUNY distinguished professor of psychology. "You can catch things as they're developing, rather than only studying them once they're already there and pretty stable.".

Following Children's Attention Over Time.

In a recent development, earlier research has linked depression with greater attention to sad faces. However, those associations have generally been modest, and scientists have not been sure whether biased attention contributes to depression or develops because of it.

The Binghamton study was designed to investigate that question by tracking both depressive symptoms and attention patterns over time. According to the researchers, it is the first study to examine how changes in each may predict later changes in the other among children.

"The real novel piece is that we looked at these transactional relations," said Kelly Gair, a PhD student at Binghamton and lead author of the paper. "Between attentional biases and depressive symptoms, we looked at the way that they were mutually predicting one another across the time points, which is especially novel and hasn't been done before.".

The research team, which also included Leslie A. Brick from the University of New Mexico, followed 242 children and their mothers for two years. Participants were assessed every six months.

Sources indicate that during each visit, children viewed pairs of faces on a screen. One face showed a neutral expression, while the other displayed an emotion (happy, sad, or angry). Eye tracking technology measured which face held the child's attention and for how long.

Children in the study looked at faces conveying different emotions onscreen, and eye tracking technology recorded where their attention veered. Photo credit: NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).

Family History Changes the Pattern.

In a recent development, the results suggest that increasing depressive symptoms do not affect every child's attention in the same way. Family history appeared to play an crucial role.

Among children whose mothers had a history of major depressive disorder, rising depressive symptoms were associated with greater attention to sad faces. In other words, as these children experienced more symptoms themselves, their attention became increasingly drawn toward expressions of sadness.

"For those who are already at risk, the more these children experience depression themselves, the more they lose their ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them," Gibb noted.

According to recent reports, "We know that when you're depressed, it changes what you pay attention to," Gair mentioned. "Our results suggest that these changes may be more long-lasting and may differ depending on family history. One thought is that for children of mothers with depression, who are exposed to more facial displays of sadness from interactions with their mom, these types of facial expressions become even more salient when they experience depression themselves, so their attention becomes increasingly stuck on sad expressions.".

Happy Faces May Lose Their Pull.

A different pattern emerged among children whose mothers had no history of depression.

When depressive symptoms increased in these children, they did not become more focused on sad expressions. Instead, they paid less attention to happy faces.

"In our lower-risk children, what seems to be happening is that experiences of depression are eroding a protective factor, which is how much they pay attention to happy faces," Gibb noted.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction suggests that depression may alter emotional attention through different pathways depending on a child's underlying level of familial risk. For some children, sadness may become increasingly difficult to ignore. For others, positive emotional signals may simply become less likely to capture their attention.

Sources indicate that the researchers are continuing to follow the children as they enter adolescence, a period when the risk of developing depression increases for many young people. They hope to determine whether these early attention patterns are associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a depression diagnosis later on.

The paper, "Transactional Relations Between Attentional Biases for Affective Stimuli and Depressive Symptoms in Offspring of Mothers With and Without Major Depressive Disorder," was published in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science.

Materials provided by Binghamton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Maybe you’ve had the experience where you’ve opened a gift that didn’t quite land… Another candle, another kitchen gadget, another book you probably won’t read.

When life can feel increasingly materialistic, receiving the gift of an experience can feel like an extra special treat. A coffee date, a class you could take together, or a simple invitation to step away from your routine for a few hours. Gifting experiences is becoming more common as people increasingly value things to do rather than things to have. Experiences create memories, prolonged joy, and ways to connect and bond with your loved ones.

Let’s explore why this trend is becoming a thoughtful option for many, and how to choose the right option for the people in your life.

It has been revealed that gifting an experience means offering someone the chance to do or enjoy something, rather than giving them a physical item. It could be a short outing, a shared class, a small adventure, or even a moment of relaxation. The focus is on creating a meaningful interaction or memory.

At its core, an experience gift acknowledges who someone is and what matters to them — comfort, curiosity, connection, or rest. It’s a way of saying, I see what brings you joy or ease, and building a shared experience around that. This can feel especially supportive for people whose lives are busy or emotionally stretched.

Because these gifts are flexible, they work across relationships and budgets. They can be shared or solo, active or restful, planned or open-ended. They offer a moment that feels nourishing and special for someone you care about.

💙 If relaxation is what they need, a Calm gift card gives them access to sleep support, meditation, and stress tools.

While research on experience gifting is still growing, studies highlight how shared time and supportive interactions can strengthen relationships and help people feel more connected.

It has been revealed that and for the giver, choosing an experience can relieve some of the pressure to pick the “perfect” item. Plus, you get to be a bit more creative since experiences can be catered to the person in question more accurately than a fresh sweater or scented bath salts.

In a recent development, these gifts also tend to linger in memory. A walk through a upcoming neighborhood, a class where you learned something together, or an afternoon spent doing something familiar but intentional can shape how people feel long after the moment ends. The emotional takeaway is often stronger than anything wrapped.

Recent findings suggest that choosing an experience gift doesn’t need to feel complicated. A few gentle questions can help you find something that feels both thoughtful and doable:.

What feels realistic for them right now?

What genuinely matches their interests?

Will this support connection in a way that feels natural?

These considerations keep the focus on care rather than wow-factor. The most memorable experience gifts are often the ones that feel easy to say yes to.

1. Slow morning together: Gift a “no-alarm morning” where you plan nothing except being together. This could look like making breakfast at home, wandering to a café, or staying in pajamas with a movie. 2. A shared learning experience: Choose a class or workshop that feels fun. Cooking, pottery, a dance class, a cocktail-making session, or even a virtual class from home. The goal is to play, not create a latest skill. Pick a time that fits your usual schedule, and make it clear there’s no pressure to be good at it. You’re just trying it out.

3. A “memory lane” date: Revisit places that matter to your relationship: where you met, a favorite early date spot, or a park you love. You can build a simple route and add tiny prompts, like sharing a favorite memory at each stop. This turns a regular outing into something personal without costing much.

4. At-home retreat night: Create a mini retreat without leaving the house. That might mean takeout, candles, phones off for a few hours, and a shared activity like a puzzle, show, or playlist swap. You can include options on a card so they can choose: a massage, a movie, a board game, or just some quiet time together.

5. Surprise “care afternoon”: Block off a few hours for them where you take on a task they’ve been dreading—organizing a small space, handling an errand, or taking something off their mental load—and then follow it with something relaxing, like a walk or coffee. The experience is both practical support and quality time.

6. Future adventure fund: If money is tight or schedules are messy, create a “future adventure” envelope. Add a small amount of money, a short list of possible outings (day trip, concert, special restaurant), and a promise to choose an option together when life settles a bit. The gift is the intention and shared planning, not just the event itself.

The Common Vitamin Linked To Less Belly Fat

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

This deeper layer of belly fat, known as visceral fat, surrounds organs such as the liver and intestines.

It matters because people with more visceral fat tend to have greater difficulty using insulin to control their blood sugar.

The link with vitamin D became weaker when the researchers took body mass index into account, suggesting that overall body size could explain part of the difference.

One possibility is that vitamin D is spread through a larger volume of tissue in people with more body fat, leaving a lower concentration in the blood.

The researchers reviewed records from nearly 1,300 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended a hospital in Quzhou, China, during a two-and-a-half-year period.

Each person had a blood test for vitamin D and a measurement to estimate their visceral fat.

The researchers divided patients into four groups according to their vitamin D levels and compared the estimated area of visceral fat in each group.

The clearest difference was between the groups with the highest and lowest vitamin D levels, with the middle groups showing a less consistent pattern.

After accounting for BMI and other differences between patients, the researchers estimated that the group with the highest vitamin D levels had about 10 square centimetres less visceral fat area than the group with the lowest levels.

Earlier research using genetic data suggested that a higher BMI can contribute to lower vitamin D levels, with weaker evidence for an effect in the other direction (Vimaleswaran et al., 2013).

As well as being distributed through a larger volume of tissue, some vitamin D may be stored in fat tissue, which could affect how much circulates in the blood.

Everyday habits could also help explain why the two measures vary together.

Someone who exercises outdoors may get more sunlight and carry less belly fat, two differences that could help explain the link.

The hospital records did not capture how much sunlight participants got, how active they were or whether they took vitamin D supplements.

Since vitamin D and belly fat were assessed at the same visit, it remains unclear which changed first or whether both were influenced by other factors.

The study was published in the Journal of International Medical Research (Zhu et al., 2026).

In a recent development, psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

Sources indicate that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy.

But when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a new name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her.

In another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.”.

In Josie’s world, being lifted is the fresh social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

Klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection.

Industry observers note that now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day-to-day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

According to recent reports, we are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today.

Recent findings suggest that klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

Sources indicate that all of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:.

Recent findings suggest that I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing. . . . As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended.

“Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”.

“It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

It has been revealed that prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for.

When I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a new sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

According to recent reports, if Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “good-enough mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik indicates, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”.

We love them because we care for them.

Beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct.

According to recent reports, in a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance.

Gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

It has been revealed that my not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration.

It has been revealed that this past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child.

The wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal.

Intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation.

On the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care.

Recent findings suggest that care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love.

It is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

Recent findings suggest that it is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

At the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate plan to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:.

Industry observers note that mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

It is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human.

Sources indicate that through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

Liza Ruggiero, M.A. , ACC, is a leadership coach, facilitator, educator, and writer whose work draws on psychology, mindfulness, and emotional intelligence to support personal and professional growth. She is the founder of Heartwork Leadership Practice, where she helps people navigating transitions, such as emerging leaders, latest parents, and career changers, develop the self-awareness and self-regard to lead from a place of purpose.

12 common physical symptoms of anxiety (and how to ease them)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • According to recent reports, anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain.
  • This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

According to recent reports, anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain. Sometimes the first sign is your heart pounding for no clear reason, or a wave of nausea before a big conversation. You might feel dizzy, short of breath, or like there’s a knot in your stomach. You’re not in immediate danger, but your body is reacting as if you are.

This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like. They can be alarming, especially if you don’t recognize them as anxiety right away. But your body responds this way for a reason, and understanding it can take some of the fear out of the experience.

Below we’ll look at the most common physical symptoms of anxiety, why they happen, and some ways to ease them.

It has been revealed that anxiety can affect your body before you've consciously registered that you're anxious at all. These are among the most common physical symptoms.

It has been revealed that 1. Racing or pounding heart (palpitations): A fast-beating or fluttering heart is one of the most recognized signs of anxiety. When your body senses a threat, it releases adrenaline, which speeds up your heart rate to pump blood to your muscles faster. This is useful when you actually need to run. Less so when you’re just checking your inbox.

Industry observers note that 2. Shortness of breath: Anxiety can make you feel like you can’t get a full breath, or like you’re slightly suffocating. Anxious breathing tends to be shallow and fast, which can lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood. This can feel scary, and anxiety is a common cause.

It has been revealed that 3. Chest tightness or pain: Muscle tension is a core part of the anxiety response and can be most noticeable in your chest, where you might feel tightness, pressure, or even mild pain. Seek emergency care if you feel sudden or severe chest pain, pain with shortness of breath or sweating, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw.

Recent findings suggest that 4. Dizziness or lightheadedness: Fast, shallow breathing can also leave you feeling faint or spaced out.

According to recent reports, 5. Tingling or numbness: Lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood can affect nerve signals and cause tingling or a pins-and-needles feeling in the hands, feet, or face. It can feel unsettling, but it’s usually short-lived. Numbness on one side of the body, sudden weakness, or trouble speaking needs urgent care.

Industry observers note that 6. Sweating: Sweating is part of the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response. Anxiety and stress can switch on your sweat glands even when you’re not hot, especially on your palms, underarms, and face.

7. Nausea or upset stomach: Your gut and brain are closely connected through the vagus nerve. When anxiety activates the stress response, digestion can slow or become disrupted. That can cause stomach upset, nausea, cramping, or an urgent need to use the bathroom.

Industry observers note that 8. Dry mouth: The stress response can slow saliva production, so many people notice a dry or sticky mouth when they’re anxious. It’s common and usually temporary, though it can make speaking feel harder than usual.

It has been revealed that 9. Muscle tension, aching, or trembling: Anxiety hormones prime your muscles to act rapidly. Sustained tension without a chance to release can cause aching, stiffness, or subtle trembling, particularly in the hands, legs, or jaw.

According to recent reports, 10. Headaches: Tension headaches often appear with anxiety and stress. They’re typically felt as a band of pressure around your head or tension in the neck and shoulders.

11. Difficulty sleeping: Anxiety and sleep tend to make each other worse. Anxious thoughts and a body that’s physically on alert make it hard to fall or stay asleep. Poor sleep, in turn, can heighten anxiety the next day, which is how the cycle keeps going.

12. Fatigue: Anxiety takes energy because running the stress response tires the body, and poor sleep or constant tension can add to it. Ongoing anxiety can leave people feeling exhausted even without much physical effort.

Industry observers note that note: Some of the above symptoms can also point to a medical condition. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or symptoms that are fresh, severe, or don’t feel like your usual anxiety, it’s best to seek medical care.

According to recent reports, anxiety triggers the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response (also known as the stress response). When your brain senses a threat, it activates the sympathetic nervous system and releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones prepare your body to respond to danger. Your heart rate increases, your breathing quickens, your muscles tense, and non-essential systems like digestion temporarily slow down.

Sources indicate that this response is useful when the threat is physical. The challenge is that your nervous system doesn’t always tell the difference between real danger and everyday stress. A tense conversation can trigger a milder version of fight-or-flight. The result is a body primed for action in situations that don’t call for it.

For most people these symptoms rise and fall with the stressful moment. When anxiety is ongoing, the symptoms can stick around longer.

There’s no instant off switch for anxiety, but these approaches can help ease physical symptoms, both in the moment and over time.

Controlled breathing can help calm the nervous system, and research suggests slow breathing helps many people feel calmer. Slow, gentle breathing, especially with a longer exhale, can shift your body toward the rest-and-digest (parasympathetic) system, which counteracts the stress response.

It has been revealed that try: Breathe in through your nose for four counts and out slowly for six. Repeat for a few minutes. You could also try box breathing, where you rhythmically hold your breath between inhales and exhales.

💙 When your body needs help slowing down, we have a short, breath-focused session for you: Breathe to Calm Down with Chibs Okereke.

Grounding techniques can help pull your attention out of anxious thoughts and back to the present moment. The 5–4–3–2–1 technique is a popular choice. To try it, notice:.

💙 If anxiety is pulling you out of your body, try Tamara Levitt's Grounding session on Calm, which guides you back to solid earth.

Recent findings suggest that exercise is well-known for easing tension, and you might find that even a short walk can take the edge off. Science agrees, with research suggesting regular exercise can help reduce anxiety symptoms over time.

It has been revealed that 💙 Not sure where to start? Try this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah on Calm to bring gentle, non-judgmental awareness to your body as it moves.

Progressive muscle relaxation involves intentionally tensing and releasing muscle groups throughout the body. It’s designed to help you relax by encouraging each muscle to unclench. It doesn’t take long, with typical sessions lasting just 10 to 20 minutes.

Sources indicate that try: Start with your feet. Tense the muscles for five seconds, then release completely. Work your way up through your calves, thighs, abdomen, hands, arms, shoulders, and face. Skip tensing any area that’s injured or painful.

It has been revealed that 💙 Not keen on the tensing? This guided Body Scan Meditation moves your attention gently through the body, one area at a time, no clenching required.

Mindfulness practices train your attention to rest on the present moment rather than looping through worries about what might happen.

Mindfulness is something you build with regular practice. Over time, it can lower how strongly your body reacts to stress, which means the physical symptoms of anxiety may appear less often, or feel less intense when they do.

💙 Work through Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety series, which is designed to help you sit with anxious feelings instead of spiraling.

Caffeine is a stimulant that can raise your heart rate and cause jitteriness, which may feel like anxiety or make it stronger.

Alcohol may feel calming at first, but it can disrupt your sleep and may make anxiety worse.

Cutting back on both is worth considering if you’re dealing with anxiety symptoms frequently.

According to recent reports, if physical symptoms of anxiety are frequent, severe, or getting in the way of daily life, talking with a doctor or mental health professional is a good next step. Effective treatments exist, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and medication when appropriate. You don’t have to manage this on your own.

Industry observers note that physical symptoms are a common part of anxiety. Anxiety activates the body’s stress response, which causes real changes like a faster heart rate, muscle tension, and altered breathing. Many people with anxiety notice at least some physical symptoms alongside the mental ones. If they’re frequent or getting in the way of daily life, it’s worth talking with a doctor or mental health professional.

“Anxiety attack” isn’t a clinical term, but people use it to describe anxiety that builds until it feels overwhelming, usually in response to a stressor like a looming deadline or a tense situation. The physical symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, muscle tension, trembling, dry mouth, dizziness, and nausea. These sensations can be distressing, but they tend to ease as the stressful situation passes or your anxiety settles.

💙 If you’ve experienced the symptoms of an anxiety attack, here’s how to recover and take care of yourself.

It has been revealed that some anxiety symptoms feel strange because the stress response affects many parts of the body at once. For example, fast breathing can cause tingling in your hands. Or you might have a feeling of unreality or disconnection (called dissociation). Muscle tension might make it feel like your throat is closing. These varied symptoms can all have anxiety as the common cause. Of course, if they’re new, intense, or don’t fit your usual anxiety symptoms, it’s best to check in with a doctor.

💙 Explore lesser-known symptoms of anxiety (some might surprise you!).

It has been revealed that when symptoms hit, the quickest relief usually comes through your breath. Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath—for example, breathing in for a count of four and out for six—and repeat for a minute or two. A longer exhale nudges your body out of the stress response and toward its rest-and-digest state.

Grounding works too. The 5–4–3–2–1 method has you name what you can see, touch, hear, smell, and taste, which pulls your focus out of anxious thoughts and back to the room around you.

According to recent reports, anxiety can affect the body as well as the mind, and for some people the physical side is what dominates, with few or no obvious worries attached. Your stress response can switch on faster than your conscious mind registers what set it off, so a racing heart or churning stomach can come before, or even without, any clear anxious thought.

These physical symptoms are still part of anxiety, and the same tools, like slow breathing and grounding, can help calm them. If they’re new or unexplained, see a doctor to rule out other causes, such as thyroid problems, heart rhythm changes, or the effects of caffeine or medication.

Sources indicate that it’s worth speaking with a doctor if your anxiety symptoms are fresh and unexplained, severe or getting worse, or affecting your day-to-day life. Some symptoms, like chest pain, shortness of breath, and heart palpitations, should be evaluated medically to rule out other causes, even if you suspect anxiety. A doctor can also refer you to a mental health professional if that would help.

If you’re experiencing sudden or severe chest pain, or chest pain with sweating, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, seek emergency care.

A worry loop is a cycle where anxiety feeds on itself. One anxious thought leads to another, and the more attention it gets, the stronger it grows.

In a recent development, for example, an anxious thought sets off a physical sensation, that sensation becomes the focus of fresh worry (“Why is my heart racing? What’s wrong with me?”), and the worry drives more symptoms.

According to recent reports, breaking the loop usually means addressing both the mind and the body. You can calm the body directly with breathing and grounding, or use cognitive approaches like CBT to interrupt the thought patterns that keep the cycle going.

Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine.
  • Researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age.
  • To investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine. The research, led by Shile Qi of the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, China, found that different conditions appear to be associated with distinct patterns of aging across the brain.

Researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age. One way to do this is with predictive age difference (PAD), which compares a person's actual age with an age estimated from brain imaging. A positive PAD means the brain appears older than would typically be expected.

To investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases. They compared those scans with data from 2,698 people with a range of conditions and differences, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), alcohol or tobacco addiction, Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.

Alzheimer's and MCI Show the Strongest Associations.

Among the conditions examined, the neurodegenerative disorders AD and MCI showed the strongest associations with higher PAD values, suggesting the greatest degree of accelerated brain aging.

Addiction and psychiatric disorders were also associated with increased PAD. By contrast, the researchers found no overall differences in PAD between controls and people with ADHD or ASD.

Different Disorders Affect Different Brain Regions.

The team also examined PAD across individual brain regions and looked at patterns of gene expression associated with the different conditions.

One area that stood out was the prefrontal cortex, which indicated higher PAD across multiple brain disorders. Psychiatric disorders were associated with elevated PAD in the frontal and temporal lobes, while dementia was linked to higher PAD in the frontal and occipital cortex.

Addiction showed a different pattern. Higher PAD was observed in the default mode network, as well as in the salience network, putamen and thalamus.

The researchers also identified differences in gene transcription associated with particular conditions and divergences, suggesting that the patterns of brain aging may be linked to distinct underlying biological processes.

A Potential Source of Future Biomarkers.

The findings do not show that these conditions directly cause accelerated brain aging. The study is correlational, and some conditions, particularly psychiatric disorders and addiction, frequently occur together, which can make their individual effects difficult to separate.

Even so, the researchers suggest that studying PAD more closely could eventually help identify biomarkers associated with common brain disorders and provide new clues about the biological pathways involved.

The authors add, "Different neurological disorders appear to leave different signatures on the brain aging clock, which may help researchers better understand the neural and biological pathways involved in these conditions.".

Sources indicate that this work was supported by the Key Research and Development Initiative of Jiangsu Province, China (BE2023668) to S.Q., and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62376124) to S.Q. The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.
