📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that neuroscientists have overturned a century-old textbook model of human language, revealing that a key speech comprehension region inside Wernicke’s area also generates an abstract “blueprint” for upcoming words a quarter-second before we speak. The study highlights that listening and speaking neurons sit side by side, opening fresh targets for neurosurgical mapping, autism research, and brain-computer interfaces that restore speech.

For more than a century, neuroscience textbooks have divided human language into two separate anatomical compartments: Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe to understand heard speech, and frontal motor circuits (such as Broca’s area and the motor cortex) to produce spoken words.

Yet that neat division never fully explained a persistent clinical paradox: why patients who suffer strokes or injuries in Wernicke’s area frequently struggle not only to comprehend language, but also to retrieve and speak the words they intend to say.

Now, in a landmark study published in Science, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) led by neurosurgeon Dr. Edward Chang have resolved that 150-year-old puzzle.

Drawing on 15 years of high-resolution intracranial brain recordings alongside targeted neural experiments, the team demonstrated that a specialized hub within Wernicke’s area actively generates a cognitive “blueprint” for each word roughly a quarter-second before a person begins to speak.

In the 1870s, German neurologist Carl Wernicke originally speculated that the posterior temporal lobe housed an “auditory image of words”, an internal template that could guide spoken output. Over subsequent decades, however, because the region sits nestled inside auditory cortex, neuroscientists largely pigeonholed it as purely a passive receiver for incoming speech sounds.

It has been revealed that “What’s different now is that we finally have the tools and the data to see the brain at the speed and scale at which speech actually happens — millisecond by millisecond, down to individual neurons,” explained co-first author Dr. Matthew Leonard, associate professor of neurological surgery at UCSF.

Combining longitudinal intracranial recordings gathered in Chang’s laboratory with new experiments designed to separate listening from speaking, Leonard and co-first author Dr. Alex Silva, a student in UCSF’s Medical Scientist Training Program, pinpointed a crucial cortical hub: the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG).

Tracking neural activity at millisecond resolution revealed that specific populations of neurons inside the lpSTG surged into action approximately 250 milliseconds (a quarter-second) before vocalization began.

Industry observers note that crucially, this pre-speech firing did not represent raw acoustic sounds or physical movements of the lips and tongue. Instead, lpSTG neurons constructed an abstract linguistic blueprint encoding:.

In a recent development, once assembled in the lpSTG, this structural blueprint traveled forward to speech-planning networks in the frontal lobe, and subsequently to the motor cortex, which translated the plan into precise articulatory muscle commands. Furthermore, high-resolution mapping showed that neurons dedicated to hearing speech sit directly beside, and sometimes overlap with, the neurons generating outgoing word blueprints.

Industry observers note that “This changes the textbook view of how the brain perceives and produces speech,” remarked Chang, chair of the UCSF Department of Neurological Surgery and member of the UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences. “Instead of being separate systems, the processes of hearing speech and actually speaking are very intertwined.”.

Housing incoming auditory processing and outgoing word planning inside the same microcircuit provides a compelling neural mechanism for how infants acquire language, converting heard sounds directly into motor-ready speech blueprints. It also offers a targeted anatomical region to investigate why roughly one-quarter to one-third of autistic children remain minimally verbal despite demonstrating strong language comprehension.

“It gives us a specific place in the brain to look, and a specific question to ask,” Chang noted.

Equally transformative are the implications for neurotechnology. Today’s speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) typically decode intended words from the motor cortex, a strategy that fails if a patient’s motor pathways are severely damaged. Because the lpSTG operates upstream of motor execution, it offers an alternative decoding gateway.

In proof-of-concept testing with two participants living with severe paralysis and anarthria (inability to speak), the UCSF team successfully decoded both the words participants attempted to say and the words they heard directly from lpSTG signals, pointing toward future conversational BCIs capable of capturing both sides of human dialogue.

How does this discovery change what we know about how the brain produces speech?

In a recent development, for over 100 years, textbooks taught that speech comprehension (Wernicke’s area) and speech production were handled by separate brain systems. UCSF researchers proved that a region inside Wernicke’s area (the lpSTG) actually activates a quarter-second before we speak to build an abstract “blueprint” of each intended word, including its length and syllable count, before sending it to motor areas.

Why can damage to Wernicke’s area make it hard to speak words, not just understand them?

Because the neurons that process heard speech sit directly alongside the neurons that build the structural blueprint for spoken words in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, a stroke or injury to that region disrupts both language comprehension and word planning.

How could this finding help paralyzed patients communicate?

Current speech brain-computer interfaces read signals from the brain’s motor cortex, which can be damaged in some paralyzed patients. Because the lpSTG creates word blueprints earlier in the speech pipeline, decoding signals from this region could restore communication for a wider range of paralyzed individuals—and potentially capture both heard and spoken words for natural conversation.

A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area.

Wernicke’s area, located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the human brain, has long been considered essential for understanding speech. However, damage to this region also disrupts the ability to produce speech, creating a long-standing puzzle in neuroscience. Traditional explanations propose that this area primarily supports speech production indirectly by monitoring sounds during speaking. However, it remains unclear whether this region plays a more direct role in generating speech itself, and if so, what kind of information it represents: sounds, movements, or even properties of whole words. Resolving this question is critical for understanding how the brain constructs language and for developing technologies to restore speech in individuals who have lost it.

Addressing this question requires probing the human brain at multiple scales with both correlational and causal methods. We combined several complementary approaches, including high-resolution direct recordings of neural populations and single neurons during speaking and listening, electrical stimulation of specific brain regions to test causality, and analysis of patients with localized brain lesions. Across these methods, participants performed a variety of speaking and listening tasks ranging from naturalistic speech to single word repetition, providing a detailed and holistic view of the role of the posterior temporal lobe in generating upcoming speech.

We identified a specific subregion within individual participants’ Wernicke’s area—the left posterior superior temporal gyrus—that becomes active before speech begins. This early activity precedes word onsets in continuous speech rather than reflecting feedback from hearing one’s own voice. Brain stimulation and lesion analyses revealed that disrupting this region causes errors in speech production, confirming its causal role.

In a recent development, detailed analyses revealed that this region encodes properties of entire words, such as their length and frequency, rather than individual sounds or motor movements. This is distinct from neighboring brain regions that encode auditory feedback and do so by representing lower-level features such as articulation or sound.

Recent findings suggest that timing analyses showed that activity in this region occurs earlier than in motor areas responsible for controlling speech muscles, placing it at the start of the speech production process. Recordings from individual neurons further confirmed that cells in this region respond before speech production, respond selectively to specific words, and are active during both speaking and listening.

Finally, in people unable to speak due to paralysis, signals from this region could be used to decode both intended and perceived speech, demonstrating its potential for multimodal brain-computer interface technologies aimed at restoring communication.

This work identifies a specialized region within Wernicke’s area that generates word-level representations before speech is produced. Rather than serving primarily as a center for speech perception, this region acts as an early stage in the production process, organizing upcoming words before they are translated into motor commands. These findings resolve a long-standing paradox about Wernicke’s area and provide a unified framework for understanding how the brain links language comprehension and production. They also highlight a promising target for future neuroprosthetic devices aimed at restoring speech in individuals with communication impairments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women.
  • Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women. The findings suggest that internalized beauty standards reshape how the brain regulates and evaluates objectifying media.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.

Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.

While behavioral studies have established that self-objectification heightens sensitivity to media portrayals, precisely how a woman’s self-perception alters the underlying neural circuitry that evaluates sexualized visuals has remained unclear.

In a study published today in eNeuro, a research team led by Zhennan Liu at Shanghai Normal University and Haoyue Qian at the Chinese Academy of Sciences investigated how individual differences in self-objectification shape both subjective beauty judgments and brain responses to sexualized imagery.

It has been revealed that the investigators recruited 60 healthy cisgender heterosexual female participants with an average age of approximately 20 years. First, the team assessed each participant’s baseline level of self-objectification using a validated psychological scale measuring how strongly individuals prioritize external appearance over internal bodily competence.

Next, participants viewed and rated a series of photographs categorized by the researchers as either:.

While participants across the board rated the sexualized photographs as more attractive than the non-sexualized images, women with higher self-objectification scores assigned significantly higher attractiveness ratings to the sexualized visuals.

When the team examined the accompanying brain activity, they uncovered a striking neural signature: women who scored higher on self-objectification exhibited dampened neural activity in brain regions involved in aesthetic judgment while assessing sexualized images.

Rather than heightened analytical engagement, this reduced activation suggests an altered regulatory or automatic evaluative response when processing culturally idealized, objectifying imagery.

“Differences between individuals [in this study] may come from how their brains regulate and evaluate the attractiveness of these images,” explained Qian.

By connecting self-objectification to measurable shifts in aesthetic evaluation circuitry, the study illustrates how internalized social standards leave a functional footprint on visual and emotional processing.

Looking ahead, the researchers aim to move beyond observational associations to test whether psychological training can buffer the brain against objectifying media.

Sources indicate that “We want to test whether experimentally training or manipulating regulation strategies (e.g., cognitive reappraisal) can change how women respond to and rate sexualized images,” Qian remarked. “This will help move the work from association toward causal and intervention-relevant questions.”.

What is “self-objectification,” and how did researchers measure it?

According to recent reports, self-objectification is the tendency to view and judge one’s own body primarily from an outside observer’s perspective, prioritizing physical appearance over internal physical capabilities. Researchers measured this trait using a validated psychological questionnaire before participants viewed media images.

How did self-objectification affect brain responses to sexualized images?

Women with higher self-objectification scores rated sexualized images of women as significantly more attractive than peers with lower scores, and showed dampened brain activity in regions responsible for aesthetic judgment, indicating differences in how their brains regulate and evaluate beauty standards.

Could psychological strategies change how the brain reacts to objectifying media?

Researchers hope to test whether training cognitive regulation techniques, such as cognitive reappraisal, which helps people consciously reframe how they interpret visual stimuli, can modify brain activity and reduce vulnerability to sexualized media representations.

Trait Self-Objectification Modulates Attractiveness-Regulating Neural Activity in Sexual Objectification Processing: An ERP Study.

Contemporary mass media frequently emphasize women’s sexual attractiveness, thereby perpetuating sexual objectification and exacerbating mental distress. Trait self-objectification is presumed to be a risk factor for these adverse outcomes; however, the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying individuals’ responses to sexual objectification remain poorly understood.

The present study examined how trait self-objectification modulates behavioral and electrophysiological responses to sexualized female images. Behaviorally, sexualized portrayals of women increased attractiveness ratings, and this enhancement was further modulated by individual levels of trait self-objectification. Neurally, processing sexualized female images evoked a set of ERPs indexing early neurocognitive processes, including perception-related N170 and EPN, and attention-related P200.

Distinct later neural responses were also identified, including the emotion-related centro-parietal LPP and the regulation-related frontal LPP (f-LPP). Among these sexual objectification-related ERP components, only the f-LPP was modulated by trait self-objectification.

Furthermore, follow-up analyses revealed that the degree to which trait self-objectification increased individuals’ attractiveness ratings of sexualized images was associated with their reduced f-LPP activity.

Collectively, these findings suggest that trait self-objectification modulates the processing of sexually objectifying stimuli by altering neurocognitive processes underlying attractiveness regulation, highlighting the importance of this regulatory mechanism in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

The cultural emphasis on women’s sexual attractiveness perpetuates sexual objectification, which is associated with adverse mental health outcomes. Trait self-objectification may modulate these outcomes, yet its relationship with the processing of sexual objectification remains unclear. This study found that trait self-objectification shapes attractiveness ratings during sexual objectification processing.

Although sexualized images elicited multiple neurocognitive components—N170 and EPN (perception-related), P200 (attention-related), cp-LPP (emotion-related), and f-LPP (regulation-related)—individual differences in trait self-objectification were selectively associated with f-LPP activity. These findings highlight the potential role of attractiveness-related regulatory processing in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

#137810. Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice

📅 12 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1990 w)

Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice

📅 12 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that what if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain?
  • The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China.
  • Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an key role in regulating aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain? Scientists investigating that possibility found that restoring a protein called Menin in older mice improved memory, balance, bone mass, and skin thickness in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing the animals with a naturally occurring amino acid improved their learning and memory in only three weeks.

The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China. Their experiments identified a previously overlooked connection between inflammation, brain chemistry, and aging throughout the body. Although the results were obtained in mice, they raised an intriguing possibility: Some effects of aging may be influenced by biological processes in the brain that scientists could eventually learn to modify.

Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an key role in regulating aging. It has also revealed why the seemingly simple supplement findings deserve careful interpretation.

How a Hidden Brain Protein May Influence Aging.

At the center of the discovery is the hypothalamus, a small but powerful region near the base of the brain. It helps regulate essential functions such as body temperature, hunger, metabolism, sleep, and hormone production. Because these systems affect nearly every organ, changes in the hypothalamus can have consequences throughout the body.

Recent findings suggest that scientists have increasingly recognized the hypothalamus as an important player in aging. One possible reason involves neuroinflammation, the brain's inflammatory response. Although inflammation helps protect against infections and injuries, persistent inflammation can interfere with normal cellular function and contribute to age-related deterioration.

Industry observers note that earlier work by Leng and colleagues had identified Menin as a protein that helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. Menin also participates in regulating gene activity, allowing it to influence multiple biological pathways.

The researchers wanted to understand what happens when this protective protein begins to disappear with age.

They discovered that Menin levels gradually declined in certain hypothalamic neurons as mice grew older. Interestingly, the same decrease was not observed in astrocytes or microglia, two other important types of brain cells involved in supporting neurons and managing immune responses.

To investigate whether this decline actually contributed to aging, the team developed genetically modified mice in which Menin could be selectively disabled.

Industry observers note that the results were striking. Mice with reduced Menin activity developed greater inflammation in the hypothalamus, thinner skin, reduced bone mass, and worsening cognitive performance. Their lifespans were also modestly shortened.

Rather than simply accompanying aging, the loss of Menin appeared capable of helping drive several of its characteristic changes.

Restoring Menin Reversed Several Signs of Aging in 30 Days.

The researchers then asked an even more interesting question: If declining Menin contributes to aging, could restoring the protein reverse some of the damage?

In a recent development, to find out, they used a gene delivery technique to increase Menin production in a specific part of the hypothalamus in older (20-month-old) mice. This region, called the ventromedial hypothalamus, helps coordinate metabolism, energy balance, and other bodily functions.

Just 30 days after treatment, the animals indicated measurable improvements.

Their skin became thicker, bone mass increased, and performance improved on tests measuring learning, memory, and balance. Researchers also observed reductions in inflammation and improvements in certain metabolic changes associated with aging.

In a separate survival analysis, mice receiving the Menin treatment also lived longer than untreated controls.

These findings suggested that some biological changes associated with old age could be at least partially reversed by restoring Menin activity in a specific group of brain cells.

But the researchers also uncovered an notable clue about how Menin produced these effects.

A Simple Amino Acid Offers a Surprising Clue.

When Menin levels declined, the researchers noticed that concentrations of D-serine, an amino acid involved in brain signaling, also fell.

It has been revealed that amino acids are best known as the building blocks of proteins, but some perform other important functions. D-serine helps regulate NMDA receptors, specialized proteins on nerve cells that are essential for communication between neurons, learning, and the formation of memories.

In a recent development, D-serine is closely related to L-serine, an amino acid commonly found in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts. The two forms have different biological roles. Although D-serine is also available as a dietary supplement, consuming ordinary serine-rich foods is not equivalent to taking the form used in the experiments.

Further investigation revealed that Menin helps control the production of PHGDH, an enzyme involved in the biochemical pathway that generates serine (which was in turn regulated by Menin). When Menin activity decreased, this pathway became less active, reducing the amount of D-serine available to the brain.

Restoring Menin increased D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a region especially important for learning and memory.

This connection suggested that the cognitive effects of declining Menin might be partly explained by disruptions in D-serine signaling.

To test the idea directly, the scientists gave older mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks.

The supplementation improved their performance on learning and memory tests, even without directly restoring Menin.

Recent findings suggest that however, there was an important distinction. While increasing Menin improved both cognitive function and physical signs of aging, D-serine supplementation primarily improved cognition. It did not restore the age-related losses in bone mass and skin thickness.

That difference suggests Menin influences aging through several biological mechanisms, with D-serine accounting for only part of its effects.

Later Research Strengthens the Link Between the Brain and Aging.

Since the original 2023 discovery, additional studies have provided evidence that the hypothalamus helps coordinate aging across the body.

According to recent reports, in a 2024 study published in Cell Metabolism, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. By maintaining or stimulating this communication pathway, they increased physical activity, improved age-related metabolic function, and extended lifespan in mice.

That work involved a different protein and neural circuit from Menin, but supported the broader idea that signals originating in the hypothalamus can influence how the rest of the body ages.

Another 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry provided additional insight into Menin itself. Researchers found that increasing Menin helped protect cultured hippocampal cells against inflammation and a form of programmed cell death triggered by exposure to the stress hormone corticosterone. Although these laboratory experiments did not establish an anti-aging effect, they supported the idea that Menin has important protective functions in brain cells.

An even larger picture emerged in January 2025, when scientists published a detailed analysis of approximately 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature.

The researchers discovered that some of the brain cells most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the hypothalamus. Many aging cells demonstrated reduced activity in genes involved in normal neuronal function and increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and immune responses.

These findings highlighted the hypothalamus as a potential center of vulnerability during brain aging, although they did not directly test the Menin pathway.

Latest Findings in 2026 Reveal More Aging Pathways.

Research published in 2026 has further strengthened the connection between hypothalamic activity and longevity.

In a recent development, in a study published in Cell, scientists found that strengthening daily biological rhythms in a specific hypothalamic region improved several aging-related measurements and extended lifespan in male mice. The intervention also reduced estimates of biological age based on DNA methylation, chemical modifications to DNA that change with age.

Another 2026 study in Cell Metabolism identified a protein called Mimecan that helps skeletal muscles communicate with the hypothalamus and brown fat, a specialized tissue involved in generating body heat. Restoring circulating Mimecan levels in older mice improved this communication and extended lifespan.

Industry observers note that together, these discoveries suggest that aging involves complex communication between the brain and the rest of the body. Rather than depending on one master switch, multiple neural circuits, hormones, and metabolic signals appear to help determine how age-related changes unfold.

Could D-Serine Supplements Protect the Human Brain?

Recent findings suggest that the possibility of improving memory with a relatively simple amino acid is especially appealing. However, evidence that D-serine can reverse age-related cognitive decline in humans remains limited.

Industry observers note that A small randomized clinical trial published in 2016 tested D-serine in 50 healthy older adults. Participants performed better on one assessment of spatial learning and problem-solving after receiving the amino acid, but researchers did not find significant improvements across the other cognitive tests or mood measurements.

More importantly, later research suggests that the effects of D-serine depend on the biological circumstances.

In an April 2025 study published in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences, scientists investigated D-serine in mice genetically engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike the Menin experiments, which associated reduced D-serine with age-related memory impairment, this study found that an early increase in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Removing the enzyme responsible for producing D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive impairments in those mice.

In a recent development, these findings do not invalidate the earlier results. Instead, they suggest that D-serine signaling is more complicated than simply having too little or too much. Its effects may depend on the condition being studied, the timing of treatment, and how the brain's signaling systems are functioning.

There are also unanswered questions about the long-term safety of D-serine supplementation. High doses have raised kidney safety concerns in animal experiments, and research has not established whether prolonged supplementation is a safe or effective way to prevent age-related memory loss in otherwise healthy people.

For now, D-serine should be considered an experimental approach rather than a proven treatment for brain aging.

Can Scientists Eventually Slow Aging by Targeting the Brain?

Despite the encouraging mouse experiments, researchers still need to answer several fundamental questions.

Why does Menin decline in the hypothalamus as animals age? How many of its effects could be reversed by treatment, and how long would those improvements last? Could restoring Menin influence other biological systems in unexpected ways?

It is also unclear whether treatments targeting Menin or D-serine could reproduce similar results in humans.

Nevertheless, the original researchers believe the pathway deserves further investigation.

According to recent reports, "We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline," mentioned Leng.

Leng adds, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes.".

According to recent reports, the growing body of evidence points toward a potentially vital shift in how scientists understand aging. Instead of viewing it only as the gradual deterioration of individual organs, researchers are investigating how specific brain pathways may actively shape the process.

Recent findings suggest that the possibility that restoring those pathways could improve memory, physical function, or longevity remains experimental. But the Menin discovery, together with subsequent findings, offers a compelling reason to explore whether some of the biological changes associated with aging are more reversible than previously thought.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that work can be tough. With only 20% of workers feeling engaged globally, we need tools that can help boost engagement and well-being at work.

While some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace. For many years, researchers have been testing different practices that individual employees, managers, and teams can do to improve work life for everyone.

According to recent reports, you can find some of these on Greater Good in Action, our library of over 100 practices found to improve well-being. Each practice includes:.

Recently, we added four latest practices that you might want to try in your workplace.

Let’s face it: We don’t always feel appreciated at work, even though appreciation seems to be a key need for most people. In this practice, you begin a regular team meeting with the simple act of appreciating the person to your left. You say something specific about one of their qualities or an action they took and the impact it had on you. Then that person appreciates the person to their left, and you go around the room (or virtual meeting) until everyone gets appreciated.

Years ago, I tested this practice in a meeting with a team I was working with. When we got to the third person being appreciated, she broke down into tears. She noted, “I’ve been working here for nine years, and I didn’t know you guys appreciate me. . . . I didn’t even know you liked me.”.

Help everyone on your team feel appreciated to boost connection and performance.

While this was hard to hear, it’s also a problem that is pretty easy to fix. Appreciation Circles, which can be repeated regularly, try to establish a culture and ritual of appreciation so that no one has to feel undervalued at work.

According to recent reports, this practice is designed for managers during their regular (and sometimes less than inspiring) one-on-one meetings with their direct reports. It recommends that you ask employees these three questions:.

As managers, sometimes we don’t realize the impact of our time with employees. Research suggests that our supportive behaviors can go a long way to helping employees feel more engaged. So how can managers be more supportive?

Improve employee satisfaction and engagement with a guided conversation.

It has been revealed that one study found that when managers encouraged, assured, and valued employee efforts, employees felt more engaged. These are the themes that the three questions in this practice address.

In a recent development, the question of how you build trust has always been a fascinating one for me, because trust is so foundational to getting things done and is such an vital part of a healthy workplace culture. Studies suggest that high-trust work cultures are often higher-performing, but how do you actually earn trust at work?

In their analysis of hundreds of studies on trust, researchers found that there are three key levers for building trust: demonstrating your ability, benevolence, and integrity. In other words, people trust you more when they believe you can get things done, have their best interests at heart, and follow through on your word.

Demonstrate your trustworthiness to your coworkers.

This practice helps you identify ways to show others that you have these qualities by considering three questions and then acting on your answers:.

This practice is probably one of the more fun and feel-good practices because it encourages you to offer some random acts of kindness to your coworkers and see if this creates a multiplier effect in your workplace.

For example, you could bring a coworker a cup of coffee, help them with a project, or offer a handwritten thank-you note.

Do something nice for coworkers and watch kindness spread.

Studies suggest that kind and helpful behaviors can be contagious to those receiving the kind acts, and that even bystanders see boosts in their well-being just from observing these acts.

We encourage you to try this low-risk and feel-good practice in your workplace soon—as well as the rest of them! Keep in touch and let us know how these practices land in your workplace.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STUDIO HERRSTRÃM rebuilds the Milkshake brand identity around car culture, a redrawn splash mark, high-vis color and road signs.

Milkshake is a Stockholm label, a division of Sony Music Entertainment founded in 2019, and its new identity starts in a car. The name was suggested on a car ride, milestones happened in cars, and new music was taken for a car test. The old splash is still there, redrawn as a rounded, blended symbol that reads like metal and liquid merging, and the wordmark runs through it with a zigzag cut that splits Milkshake into two stacked hits. On the posters the name fills the frame until the letters stop being text and start being the picture: acid yellow Milksh across the top, shake across the bottom.

The type system is Gates, a neo-grotesque from Contextype, shown in the specimen with arrows, asterisks, circled letters and roman numerals on a mauve field. The wordmark itself leans forward, its letters cut on a slant that matches the splash, and the supporting lockups borrow their logic from car window stickers and milk carton nutrition labels: small blocks of capitals that hold track names, release dates and the p-line symbol without breaking the grid.

The system proves itself on the objects it touches. A high-vis vest carries the full lockup on its back in black on acid yellow, with reflective bands borrowed from road markings. A neon green acrylic cube hangs outside the shopfront with the black wordmark on its face. A blender wears the whole icon set as stickers: the machine that makes the drink becomes the merch.

In a recent development, color does the rest. Acid yellow is the signal color, while neon pink and soft lilac take the flavor cues and black keeps the contrast high. The same palette runs the subway poster for Tove Lo's single Me/You (always and forever), dated 18.09.26. Linn Wexell, founder and creative director of Milkshake, says the creative work was smart and on point and the visuals stunning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.

Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.

People with higher vitamin D levels tend to sleep longer and have more consistent sleep patterns.

Those with higher levels also tend to spend a greater proportion of their time in bed asleep.

One proposed explanation involves melatonin, the hormone that helps signal when it is time to sleep.

The findings suggest that vitamin D status and sleep may be connected through other biological processes or shared everyday habits.

The research involved almost 80 generally healthy adults aged 18 to 45, recruited from the University of Delaware and the surrounding area.

Participants wore wrist monitors for two weeks, allowing researchers to estimate their sleep duration and timing.

Blood tests measured vitamin D levels, while urine samples provided an indicator of overnight melatonin production.

Before statistical adjustments, people whose vitamin D levels were 10 ng/mL higher slept around 12 minutes longer per night.

The association with longer sleep remained across the adjusted analyses, although several other links weakened.

Because the research was observational, it cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D improves sleep.

Sleep follows an internal rhythm that repeats roughly every 24 hours.

Light reaching the eyes helps the brain keep this rhythm aligned with the cycle of day and night.

As darkness falls, the brain normally increases its release of melatonin, helping the body prepare for sleep.

Bright artificial light late in the evening can interfere with this process and delay that signal.

Time spent outdoors and physical activity can also influence these rhythms.

Sunlight has another role in the body, allowing exposed skin to produce vitamin D.

People who spend little time outside may have more difficulty obtaining enough of the vitamin.

Food provides another source, particularly oily fish such as salmon and mackerel, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Previous research offers some evidence that vitamin D supplements may improve how people rate their sleep quality (Abboud, 2022).

A review brought together 19 intervention studies, although only three trials could be combined in its main statistical analysis.

Those trials found improvements in questionnaire scores after supplementation, but participants included people with fibromyalgia and those receiving methadone treatment.

Results for sleep duration and specific sleep disorders were less consistent, leaving questions about who might benefit and which aspects of sleep could change.

The study was published in the journal SLEEP Advances (D’Agata et al., 2025).

Tech Report: Does Working Harder Make Learning Fun?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable.
  • Parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it.
  • Yet a new psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable. Three experiments reveal that while cognitive effort improves comprehension, it does not spark curiosity or enjoyment, instead, preexisting interest motivates students to engage in the first place.

Parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it. Behind this common wisdom lies an intuitive assumption that sustained cognitive effort naturally blossoms into curiosity and intrinsic motivation.

Yet a new psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.

Published in Acta Psychologica, the study demonstrates that forcing effort improves basic comprehension, but it does not make dry or unappealing material more interesting. Instead, genuine interest and liking come first—serving as the psychological spark that motivates learners to invest cognitive effort voluntarily.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m curious if a student is made to work harder, does that bring the same benefits as effort they choose to give,” asked Yimeng Jin, a doctoral student at Kyushu University’s Graduate School of Systems Life Sciences and first author of the study. “It matters because many learning environments rely on required effort, such as assignments, on the assumption that more effort is always better.”.

To disentangle voluntary motivation from mandatory mental exertion, Jin and senior author Professor Johan Lauwereyns at Kyushu University’s Faculty of Arts and Science conducted three behavioral experiments involving 110 university students.

Participants read pairs of seemingly unrelated sentences and decided whether they wanted to construct an explanation connecting them. By tracking participants’ initial choices, task completion, and time spent, the team isolated two distinct components of learning: willingness to engage and cognitive effort invested.

Across the three experimental phases, a clear cognitive pattern emerged:.

In a recent development, “Interestingly, participants who were required to explain spent more time on the task than those who chose to do so,” Jin noted. “Perhaps they initially skipped it because the sentences were harder to understand, so they needed more time to make sense of them. It’s a bit like struggling through homework in a subject you don’t enjoy. Together, the experiments suggest that effort can help people make sense of information, while interest is more closely linked to their willingness to engage.”.

While the researchers caution that short laboratory reading tasks among university students differ from long-term classroom learning in younger children, the findings carry broad implications for how educators, parents, and communicators design learning environments. Rather than relying solely on mandatory drill work to manufacture enthusiasm, sparking authentic curiosity first may unlock deeper, faster comprehension.

“The findings have implications far outside education. The connection between engagement and effort is key whenever our understanding depends on reading texts,” concluded Lauwereyns.

Does working harder on a subject automatically make it more enjoyable?

Industry observers note that no. Researchers at Kyushu University found that while putting in cognitive effort helps students better understand difficult material, it does not increase their interest in or enjoyment of the subject.

What actually motivates students to put effort into learning?

According to recent reports, the experiments highlighted that preexisting interest and liking come first. When students already find a topic intriguing, they are far more willing to engage voluntarily, and they comprehend the material more efficiently than when forced to work through topics they want to skip.

What happens when students are forced to work on material they don’t find interesting?

When participants were required to explain material they initially chose to skip, they spent significantly more time struggling with the task, gained less comprehension compared to voluntary effort, and revealed no increase in enjoyment.

Effort enhances understanding, while appreciation drives engagement in Cross-sentence semantic processing.

It has been revealed that comprehensive reading requires active semantic processing, going beyond explicitly stated information to construct connections and meaning. Building on discourse coherence theory, Reader-Response Theory and insights from Language Poetry, the present research investigates how active engagement and cognitive effort shape semantic processing.

We propose that evaluative dimensions central to aesthetic appreciation, namely understanding, interest, and liking, also play crucial roles in semantic processing.

To examine these processes, we developed a novel cross-sentence elaboration paradigm using unconnected, randomly paired sentences that create semantic gaps and encourage reader-driven meaning construction.

Sources indicate that in Experiment 1, participants could voluntarily invest effort by thinking aloud during elaboration. Results highlighted greater volitional engagement was associated with higher levels of understanding, interest, and appreciation.

Experiment 2 dissociated willingness to engage from actual effort, revealing that appreciation predicted participants’ willingness to invest further effort, whereas additional completed effort did not consistently increase appreciation.

Experiment 3 examined forced effort, showing that externally imposed effort enhanced semantic understanding but did not consistently increase appreciation, highlighting the distinct roles of volitional and imposed effort.

An integrated 2 × 2 analysis of Experiments 2 and 3 demonstrated that active engagement and cognitive effort made distinct, interactive contributions to evaluation and processing time, with completed cognitive effort more reliably predicting accurate recognition memory and active engagement more closely tied to memory for the processing context.

Together, these findings clarify the interplay between engagement, effort, understanding, and appreciation, offering fresh insights into the cognitive dynamics of active meaning construction in semantic processing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins. Yet another essential part of brain biology has received far less attention: lipids. These fatty molecules make up the membranes surrounding neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation that protects nerve fibers, and play important roles in communication between brain cells.

Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located. Conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the brain's chemical organization.

It has been revealed that "So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," claims Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL. "That gap matters, because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease.".

Researchers at EPFL have now taken a major step toward filling that gap. A team led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno has created a detailed map showing how lipids are distributed throughout the mouse brain.

Recent findings suggest that their Lipid Brain Atlas reveals that these molecules are arranged in highly organized patterns. Some match familiar anatomical structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches had overlooked. The patterns are so distinctive that researchers could identify where a brain tissue sample originated simply by examining its lipid composition.

The findings were published in Nature.

Scientists Identify 539 Distinct Chemical Zones in the Brain.

To construct the atlas, researchers used mass spectrometry imaging, a technique that allows them to identify lipid molecules across thin sections of brain tissue. A laser scans each slice one location at a time, producing detailed information about which lipids are present and where they are found.

The team examined 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices collected from 11 mice. This generated approximately 7 million measurements, which scientists combined into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed specifically for the project.

The resulting atlas revealed 539 chemically distinct territories, which the researchers named "lipizones." Each has a characteristic combination of lipids, creating a recognizable chemical signature.

In a recent development, many of these regions correspond to established brain structures and cell types. Others reveal unexpected relationships between groups of nerve cell bodies and distant regions connected by their fibers. Such connections have often been difficult to detect using maps based on gene activity.

"In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address," indicates D'Angelo.

Hidden Chemical Patterns Challenge Previous Brain Maps.

The upcoming atlas also uncovered surprising differences within parts of the brain that scientists previously considered relatively uniform.

In a recent development, one striking example is white matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. Rather than having a largely consistent chemical composition, white matter contains numerous distinct lipid zones.

"This highlights that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, the structure responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.

Together, these findings show that lipid mapping can reveal key features of brain organization that are not apparent from anatomy or genetic information alone.

Pregnancy Triggers Widespread Changes in Brain Lipids.

Beyond identifying the brain's chemical structure, the atlas offered fresh insight into how that structure changes during pregnancy.

When researchers examined pregnant mice, they found substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions. Overall, these changes were more pronounced than the typical lipid differences observed between male and female mice.

According to recent reports, the cortex, which forms the brain's outer layer, revealed particularly extensive changes. Meanwhile, levels of galactosyl ceramide, an notable component of myelin, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter.

These findings suggest that pregnancy involves significant changes in the brain's chemical makeup, potentially helping its neural connections adapt to the body's changing demands.

"Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy," says Gioele La Manno. "The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs.".

A Newly introduced Tool for Understanding Brain Aging and Disease.

The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists worldwide to explore this previously difficult-to-study aspect of brain biology.

By combining lipid information with existing genetic and cellular maps, researchers can gain a more complete understanding of how the brain is organized and how its chemistry changes over time.

The atlas also establishes a detailed reference for healthy mouse brain tissue. Scientists can use it to investigate how disruptions in lipid distribution might contribute to brain development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression.

Although the specific mouse brain map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach used to create it could help researchers uncover comparable patterns in the human brain.

"What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers dramatically accelerated electron tomography to map large volumes of brain tissue at 15-nanometer 3D resolution.
  • Sources indicate that to understand how billions of neurons orchestrate thoughts, memories, and movement, neuroscientists construct connectomes, detailed wiring diagrams mapping how brain cells connect and communicate.
  • As a result, even the most ambitious brain wiring maps have routinely missed ultra-fine cellular architectures, including electrical synapses (also called gap junctions), microscopic channels that enable direct, near-instantaneous electrical communication between adjacent neurons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers dramatically accelerated electron tomography to map large volumes of brain tissue at 15-nanometer 3D resolution. The breakthrough captures fine neural structures missed by conventional connectomes, including rapid-fire electrical synapses and uncharacterized protrusions where neurons appear to “nibble” neighboring glial cells.

Sources indicate that to understand how billions of neurons orchestrate thoughts, memories, and movement, neuroscientists construct connectomes, detailed wiring diagrams mapping how brain cells connect and communicate. While macro-scale MRI scans chart major white-matter highways and standard electron microscopy traces individual chemical synapses, scaling up to large tissue volumes has historically forced a difficult compromise: sacrificing nanoscale structural detail for imaging speed.

As a result, even the most ambitious brain wiring maps have routinely missed ultra-fine cellular architectures, including electrical synapses (also called gap junctions), microscopic channels that enable direct, near-instantaneous electrical communication between adjacent neurons.

Now, in a study published November 19 in Nature Methods, researchers at Harvard Medical School (HMS) and the University of California San Diego have overcome that bottleneck by supercharging electron tomography—a 3D imaging technique that reconstructs nanoscale architecture by tilting tissue samples and capturing views from multiple angles.

It has been revealed that led by co-senior authors Dr. Wei-Chung Allen Lee (associate professor of neurobiology at HMS and associate professor of neurology at Boston Children’s Hospital) and Dr. Mark Ellisman (UC San Diego), alongside co-first authors Dr. Aaron T. Kuan and Dr. Sébastien Phan, the team demonstrated that large blocks of brain tissue can be mapped in exquisite 3D nanoscale detail without prohibitive imaging times.

According to recent reports, conventional electron tomography is painstakingly slow because it typically requires capturing hundreds of tilted images across razor-thin tissue slices. By refining image acquisition and computational reconstruction, Lee, Ellisman, and colleagues discovered they could cut the required number of images by roughly 50-fold while imaging tissue sections 20 times thicker than standard electron microscopy protocols, preserving an extraordinary 3D resolution of 15 nanometers or finer.

Sources indicate that “We can now see brain structures that we haven’t been able to see before in connectomics data,” explained Lee. “We hope this work will help us understand how nervous systems are built; what changes with age; and what goes awry in neurodevelopmental, cognitive, and neurodegenerative disorders.”.

When the researchers applied their high-speed tomography pipeline to tissue from the mouse cerebellum, the 3D reconstructions revealed both long-sought neural connections and surprising cellular behaviors:.

“We’re seeing uncharacterized structures, suggesting that neurons are ‘nibbling’ their neighboring cells,” Lee said.

In addition, the researchers traced delicate nerve fibers continuously through the thick 3D tissue block right down to their exact synaptic contact points with target neurons.

While scaling this accelerated tomography workflow to map an entire mammalian brain will require automated tissue-handling robotics, the breakthrough bridges a critical resolution gap in modern connectomics—equipping neuroscientists to examine how fine electrical and glial-neuronal connections form in early life and break down in brain disease.

Why do traditional brain wiring maps (connectomes) miss certain structures?

Recent findings suggest that mapping large volumes of brain tissue at high speed usually forces scientists to sacrifice ultra-fine resolution. As a result, critical microscopic features, such as tiny electrical synapses (gap junctions) that connect neurons directly, often blur out or go undetected in large-scale datasets.

How did researchers speed up nanoscale 3D brain imaging?

The team optimized electron tomography so that it requires about 50 times fewer multi-angle images on tissue slices 20 times thicker than usual, while still maintaining a 3D resolution of 15 nanometers or finer.

What surprising new structures did they see in the brain tissue?

Alongside hard-to-see electrical synapses in the mouse cerebellum, the researchers discovered tiny protrusions between neurons and neighboring support cells (glia), suggesting that neurons physically “nibble” or take up material from adjacent cells.

Funding: This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants RF1MH129261, U01NS142013, and K99EB032217), with startup support to Kuan from the Yale School of Medicine Department of Neuroscience and Wu Tsai Institute.

According to recent reports, harvard University filed a patent application regarding GridTape (WO2017184621A1) on behalf of inventors, including Lee, and negotiated licensing agreements with interested partners. All other authors have no competing interests.

Scalable electron tomography for connectomics.

We demonstrate limited-tilt, serial-section electron tomography (ET), which can non-destructively map brain circuits over large 3D volumes and provide high-resolution, supramolecular details within subvolumes of interest.

Here we show accelerated ET imaging of semi-thick sections ( >500 nm) from the mouse cerebellar cortex, with 3D resolution <15 nm and machine learning-based image augmentation, providing the capacity to resolve key features of neuronal circuits including chemical synapses, endocytic structures and gap junctions.

Furthermore, we systematically assess how imaging parameters affect image quality and speed to enable connectomic-scale projects.

Scientists Build 6,986 Digital Brain Twins to Study Dementia

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an international consortium has created personalized biophysical “digital brain twins” for 6,986 individuals across 16 countries to uncover how aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and environmental conditions shape neural dynamics.
  • Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an invaluable window into the living human brain, yet it records only indirect proxies of neural activity, typically relying on group averages that obscure individual variation and say little about the underlying cellular mechanisms driving those signals.
  • In a recent development, now, an international research team led by corresponding author Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an international consortium has created personalized biophysical “digital brain twins” for 6,986 individuals across 16 countries to uncover how aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and environmental conditions shape neural dynamics. The computational models simulate excitation-inhibition balance across 90 connected brain regions, revealing distinct mechanistic signatures for Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal degeneration, and environmental exposures ranging from air pollution to democratic governance.

Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an invaluable window into the living human brain, yet it records only indirect proxies of neural activity, typically relying on group averages that obscure individual variation and say little about the underlying cellular mechanisms driving those signals.

In a recent development, now, an international research team led by corresponding author Dr. Agustín Ibáñez (Scientific Director of BrainLat at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, strategic director of core scientific assets at the BarcelonaBeta Brain Research Center, and faculty at the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin) and first author Dr. Rubén Herzog (BrainLat and Distinguished Professor at the University of the Balearic Islands) has transformed static brain scans into dynamic, personalized virtual laboratories.

Published today in Nature Biomedical Engineering, the study introduces biophysical “digital brain twins” constructed from resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) scans of 6,986 individuals spanning ages 18 to 100 across 16 countries.

Rather than treating brain scans as passive statistical snapshots, biophysical brain twins apply mathematical equations grounded in neurobiology to simulate how populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons interact across 90 connected brain regions.

For each participant, the investigators tuned their computational model until its simulated fMRI output closely matched the individual’s actual resting-state brain recordings. Independent validation demonstrated that model-derived regional excitability closely correlated with structural grey matter volume, confirming that the virtual simulations capture real biological architecture.

Recent findings suggest that “Every brain ages in a different context. Our biophysical twins help us study how the variations in our biology and the social and environmental conditions of our lives relate to brain function,” explained Ibáñez. “The importance of biophysical brain twins is that they connect what brain scans record with the underlying processes that could produce those signals. Each twin acts as a personalised virtual laboratory: researchers can adjust how its neural populations interact and examine how those changes affect the whole brain. This opens a route from observing differences to testing possible explanations, mechanisms, potential treatments and interventions.”.

“MRI records indirect measures of neural activity. Biophysical twins let us simulate the neural processes that might generate those signals and explore why they differ from person to person,” added Herzog.

Applying these nearly 7,000 personalized models across diverse clinical cohorts exposed clear mechanistic boundaries between normal aging and dementia:.

To overcome the historical divide between neuroimaging and real-world lived context, the team linked individual brain models with macro-level environmental indicators across 10 domains alongside personal socioeconomic histories.

Recent findings suggest that robust associations emerged in seven of the ten environmental domains, most prominently in indicators measuring democratic conditions (free choices, civic participation, political representation, and rule of law), soil and water quality, and air pollution. Complementary analyses of individual life circumstances further linked brain dynamics to healthcare access, childhood experiences, and financial stability. These relationships persisted even after controlling for age, sex, clinical diagnosis, country, and MRI scanner hardware.

It has been revealed that by releasing their open-source code and model parameters, the authors have established a global testbed for in silico experimentation. Future studies can overlay neurotransmitter receptor maps onto these digital twins—simulating how targeted modulation of glutamate (excitatory) or GABA (inhibitory) signaling, or public health improvements in air quality and healthcare access, might shift an aging brain back toward healthy functional patterns.

What is a biophysical “digital brain twin”?

It has been revealed that A digital brain twin is a personalized computer simulation built from an individual’s fMRI scan using biological equations. By modeling how 90 connected brain regions interact, it allows researchers to estimate underlying cellular processes, such as the balance between signals that excite or inhibit neurons—and test virtual treatments safely on a computer.

How do brain dynamics differ between normal aging and dementia?

Sources indicate that in the study of nearly 7,000 people, normal aging primarily changed how regularly or unpredictably brain activity fluctuated over time. In contrast, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal degeneration disrupted overall activity levels, variability, and the balance between excitatory and inhibitory brain signals all at once.

Can environmental and social conditions really affect how the brain functions?

Recent findings suggest that yes. Even after accounting for age, sex, diagnosis, and scanner differences, researchers found that environmental factors, especially democratic conditions, soil and water quality, air pollution, healthcare access, and financial circumstances, were measurably linked to underlying simulated brain dynamics.

Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype–expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.

Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological–environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics.

Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia.

Sources indicate that personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure–function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes.

Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research.

These findings ground phenotypic–exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

Industry News: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, feeling overwhelmed by stress or struggling to adjust when things go wrong?
  • Newly introduced research from Binghamton University suggests that these healthy routines are connected to a mental skill called psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to challenges and recover from stressful experiences.
  • Industry observers note that psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, feeling overwhelmed by stress or struggling to adjust when things go wrong? Everyday habits such as eating a nutritious breakfast, getting regular exercise, and sleeping enough may play an key role in how well your mind handles difficult situations.

Newly introduced research from Binghamton University suggests that these healthy routines are connected to a mental skill called psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to challenges and recover from stressful experiences.

Industry observers note that psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change. Rather than becoming trapped in negative thinking or overwhelmed by frustration, people with greater psychological flexibility can recognize their emotions, consider their options, and respond in a more productive way.

In a recent development, "You might know someone who stays cool under pressure," said Lina Begdache, an associate professor of health and wellness studies at Binghamton University and lead author of the research. "The kind of person who misses a flight and, instead of panicking, calmly adapts to the situation. This person may still feel stressed, but they're better able to manage it through psychological flexibility.".

"People may say that these are resilient people, but they also have what's called psychological flexibility. They're able to change the way they think about the situation and then use brain resources to handle the stress.".

How Breakfast, Sleep, and Exercise Relate to Mental Resilience.

It has been revealed that to explore the relationship between lifestyle choices and emotional resilience, Begdache worked with Jason Cherry, a former Binghamton assistant professor of physical therapy, and former student Alexander J. Talkachov.

The researchers collected anonymous survey responses from approximately 400 college students, gathering information about their diets, sleep patterns, exercise habits, and other lifestyle factors.

Their findings revealed an key connection between healthy routines and the ability to cope with stress. Students who reported healthier habits, including regular physical activity and consistent breakfast consumption, also tended to demonstrate greater psychological flexibility and resilience.

The study identified several notable associations:.

The opposite pattern also emerged. Students who reported less healthy behaviors, including frequent fast food consumption and insufficient sleep, tended to show greater psychological rigidity, meaning they had more difficulty adjusting their thoughts and behaviors when circumstances changed.

Because the research relied on survey responses, the results demonstrate associations rather than proving that these habits directly improve psychological flexibility or resilience.

Why Psychological Flexibility Matters for Stress.

According to Begdache, psychological flexibility gives people the mental space to recognize what they are experiencing instead of becoming completely absorbed by their stress. This ability to reassess a situation can make it easier to understand difficult emotions and determine how to respond.

She explained that improvements in diet and lifestyle may help support this kind of mental adaptability.

Industry observers note that "When we're under stress, we feel like we fuse with the stress. We live the stress. But psychological flexibility is like stepping back and thinking, 'I feel this because of that. What can I do?' Identifying your emotions sometimes helps you find the solution for these emotions," remarked Begdache.

The findings also build on Begdache's previous research, which linked nutritious diets to greater resilience and poorer dietary habits to reduced resilience.

Recent findings suggest that the latest study offers a possible explanation for that relationship. Rather than influencing resilience alone, diet and lifestyle may support psychological flexibility, which in turn helps people manage stress more effectively.

Industry observers note that "The upcoming finding here is that diet and lifestyle don't just make you resilient by themselves. They help you build the psychological flexibility, which, in turn, makes you a resilient person.".

The study, "Dietary and lifestyle factors and resilience: the role of psychological flexibility as a mediator," was published in the Journal of American College Health.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
